analysis.one_liner: Requires overtime pay after 32 hours a week instead of 40, phased in over four years.
analysis.headline: Senator Sanders introduced the bill with zero cosponsors, and it has sat in the Senate labor committee with no hearing or vote since September 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the standard workweek from 40 hours to 32. Employers would owe time-and-a-half pay for hours beyond 32 in a week (double time past 12 hours in a day), with the new threshold phased in over about four years. It also bars employers from cutting a worker's weekly pay or benefits because of the change, so many workers would keep the same paycheck while working fewer hours.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers who regularly put in long weeks. Anyone working past 32 hours would either earn overtime premiums or, because the bill forbids pay cuts, work fewer hours at the same weekly pay. Workers on long shifts would get time-and-a-half after 8 hours in a day and double time after 12. Roughly 3.5 years after passage, the 32-hour standard would be fully in effect.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers putting in long weeks

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the overtime threshold from 40 hours a week to 32, so time worked beyond 32 hours must be paid at one-and-a-half times the regular rate.
Adds daily overtime on top of weekly overtime: one-and-a-half times pay after 8 hours in a workday and double pay after 12 hours.
Phases the lower threshold in over roughly four years for workers covered by the amended provision: 38 hours the first year, then 36, then 34, then 32.

Bars employers from reducing a covered worker's total weekly compensation or benefits because the worker is newly covered by the overtime rules, meaning workers keep their weekly pay even if their scheduled hours shrink.
Applies the 32-hour standard to the special hospital workweek rule, which currently allows longer schedules over a two-week period.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on long hours from hourly staff — retail stores, restaurants, hospitals, nursing homes, manufacturers, and warehouses — would owe premium pay for hours past 32 a week (or past 8 a day) or restructure schedules and hire more staff. Some of that cost would likely show up in prices, and small businesses with thin margins would feel it most. Workers who want more than 32 hours would need their employer to pay the premium.

drawbacks.text: The costs fall on employers, who would either pay premium wages for hours past 32, cap workers' hours, or hire more staff; many would pass some of it to customers through higher prices.

The new daily rule (overtime after 8 hours in a day, double time after 12) would force changes to scheduling in industries like healthcare and food service that depend on long shifts, and could lead employers to spread hours across more part-time workers.
Workers who want or need more than 32 hours of work would find employers far more reluctant to schedule them, since every extra hour now carries a 50% or 100% pay premium.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For hourly workers, the upside is real and concrete: premium pay for long weeks and days, plus a legal guarantee that weekly pay cannot be cut when hours are reduced. The costs are genuine too — higher labor bills for employers in sectors that run long shifts, likely some price increases, and less scheduling flexibility for workers who want extra hours. The multi-year phase-in softens the shock for employers. The honest tradeoff is a shift of income and time toward hourly workers, paid for mainly by the businesses that employ them and, in part, by consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and has had no hearing, vote, or cosponsors since.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill in the Senate on September 14, 2026, where it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee has taken no further action — no markup, hearing vote, or floor schedule appears in the record — and the congressional session ends January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that depend on long hourly workweeks are better off so far, because the bill has gone nowhere and the overtime costs it would impose have never come close to a vote. Hourly workers have gained nothing, but also lost nothing beyond the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that rely on long hours

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and got it referred to the HELP Committee.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote in the record.

against.name: Every other sitting senator
against.what_they_did: None signed on as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: There have been no votes, and no senator from either party joined as a cosponsor, so the partisan shape is untested — though the absence of even one cosponsor suggests no appetite in either caucus.

industries.note: These employers run long hourly shifts and would owe premium pay past 32 hours a week or 8 hours a day, or else restructure staffing. Their interest in stopping the bill runs directly against the wage gain for their workers.

The bill tightens the special hospital workweek rule and adds daily overtime, hitting sectors that depend on 12-hour and overnight shifts. Resistance here means keeping long-shift staffing arrangements that the bill would make much more expensive.
Small employers with thin margins would bear the same premium-pay rules as large ones, with less ability to absorb or restructure around them.

analysis.trajectory: With roughly three and a half months left in the session, zero cosponsors, and no committee action of any kind, the bill is almost certain to expire in committee without a hearing or vote. Similar workweek bills Sanders has introduced in past congresses never advanced, and nothing in this record suggests a different path.
